title: Binary search explained: how it works, Python code and complexity — cv.cm
description: Binary search finds a value in a sorted list in O(log n) steps by halving the range. Step-by-step trace, Python code, bisect, variants and off-by-one bugs.
h1: Binary search explained: how it works, code and complexity
answer: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array by repeatedly checking the middle element and discarding the half that cannot contain the target. Each step halves the search range, so it needs at most about log₂ n + 1 comparisons: 20 for a million items. It runs in O(log n) time and O(1) extra space, but only works on data that is sorted (or, more generally, monotonic).

body: Linear search checks items one by one and needs up to n comparisons. If the data is sorted, you can do much better: compare the target with the middle item, and you immediately know which half to keep. This is the same idea as looking up a word in a paper dictionary.

Binary search also works on anything that is monotonic, not only arrays. If a yes/no condition is false for all small values and true for all large ones, binary search finds the boundary. This is called binary search on the answer.
Search for 23 in the sorted list `[2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]` (indexes 0 to 9). Keep two indexes, `lo` and `hi`, that bound the range still to be checked.
Three comparisons instead of six for a linear scan. For a list of a million items, binary search needs at most 20.
The iterative version below uses a closed range `[lo, hi]`: both ends are still candidates. The loop runs while the range is not empty.

In real Python code, use the standard library module `bisect`. `bisect_left` returns the leftmost position where the target could be inserted while keeping the list sorted, which also tells you whether it is present.

body.code:
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right, insort
data = [1, 3, 3, 3, 7, 9]
i = bisect_left(data, 3)
print(i, bisect_right(data, 3))   # 1 4  (3 occupies indexes 1..3)
print(i < len(data) and data[i] == 3)   # True: 3 is present
print(bisect_left(data, 5))       # 4: insertion point for 5
insort(data, 5)
print(data)                       # [1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 7, 9]

body.note: Binary search requires a sorted array with O(1) access by index. On a linked list, reaching the middle costs O(n), which removes the benefit. Sorting first costs O(n log n), so for a single lookup on unsorted data, a linear scan is cheaper.

sections.h: Variants: first, last and binary search on the answer
body: Many problems ask not whether a value exists but where a boundary is: the first index with a value at least x, the last occurrence of x, or the smallest number that satisfies a condition. Use a half-open range `[lo, hi)` and never stop early.

body.code:
def first_true(lo, hi, ok):
    """Smallest x in [lo, hi) with ok(x) True, or hi if none.
    ok must be False...False True...True over the range."""
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid):
            hi = mid          # mid may be the answer, keep it
        else:
            lo = mid + 1      # mid is too small
    return lo
data = [1, 3, 3, 3, 7, 9]
print(first_true(0, len(data), lambda i: data[i] >= 3))   # 1
# Integer square root of 200: largest x with x*x <= 200
print(first_true(0, 201, lambda x: x * x > 200) - 1)      # 14

ul: Lower bound (first index with value ≥ x): `bisect_left`.
Upper bound (first index with value > x): `bisect_right`.
Count of x in a sorted list: `bisect_right(a, x) - bisect_left(a, x)`.
Search in a rotated sorted array, peak finding and minimizing a maximum (for example, the smallest capacity that ships all packages in D days) are classic interview variants.
Mixing range conventions. With a closed range use `lo <= hi` and `hi = mid - 1`; with a half-open range use `lo < hi` and `hi = mid`. Mixing them causes infinite loops or skipped elements.
Writing `lo = mid` instead of `lo = mid + 1`. When `hi = lo + 1`, mid equals lo and the loop never ends.
Running binary search on unsorted data. It returns wrong answers without any error.
Integer overflow in `(lo + hi) / 2` in languages with fixed-size integers such as Java, C and C++. Use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`. Python integers do not overflow, so `(lo + hi) // 2` is safe.
Returning the first match found when the task asks for the first occurrence among duplicates.

body: Real-world uses include database and file-system indexes (B-trees generalize the idea), `git bisect` for finding the commit that introduced a bug, looking up a value in a sorted table of ranges such as IP blocks, and many numeric problems where you search for a threshold.

faq.q: What is the time complexity of binary search?
faq.a: O(log n) in the average and worst case, and O(1) in the best case. Each comparison halves the remaining range, so 1,000,000 items need at most 20 comparisons.

faq.q: Does binary search need a sorted array?
faq.a: Yes. The array must be sorted by the same order you compare with, or the condition you test must be monotonic. On unsorted data the result is unreliable.

faq.q: What does bisect do in Python?
faq.a: The `bisect` module performs binary search on sorted lists. `bisect_left` and `bisect_right` return insertion points, and `insort` inserts while keeping the list sorted (the search is O(log n), the insertion itself is O(n)).

faq.q: Is recursive or iterative binary search better?
faq.a: The iterative version is usually preferred because it uses O(1) space and avoids recursion overhead. The recursive version is equally correct and uses O(log n) stack space.

faq.q: Why does binary search use lo + (hi - lo) / 2?
faq.a: In languages with fixed-size integers, `lo + hi` can overflow when both are large. `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` gives the same middle without overflow. In Python this is not needed.
